\begin{abstract}
How well can a dealer forecast the largest absolute recorded net position before a reporting horizon ends? Such forecasts motivate evaluating a monitoring input for the measured position series. We compare historical peak constructions with ridge quantile regression and local quantiles on a market maker's FX client-flow series and a weekly Treasury-dealer aggregate. The common target includes the observed issue position and uses completed training labels. First, six-record FX regression lowers matched-history pinball loss by 14.77\%, while breaches rise from 360 to 376. Second, the Treasury primary deteriorates by 50.79\%, with breaches rising from 28 to 54. Third, lower pinball loss often accompanies more breach occasions. The evidence is specific to the inspected records, stipulated score and source-measurement conventions.

\section*{1. Introduction}
Dealers absorb customer order imbalances while managing inventory risk and scarce balance-sheet capacity. Inventory affects optimal dealer pricing (Ho and Stoll, 1981), FX dealing (Lyons, 1995), and observed inventory adjustment in dealership markets (Hansch, Naik and Viswanathan, 1998). Treasury intermediation likewise depends on dealer capacity (Duffie et al., 2023). A forecast of the maximum recorded position magnitude over a future horizon may support monitoring of the measured position: an endpoint can return toward its starting value after an intervening large position. Translating that monitoring signal into a particular margin or financing decision requires the corresponding contractual and balance-sheet inputs.

We ask whether mature conditional estimators improve forecasts of an absolute sampled-position peak relative to simple historical constructions. Every procedure predicts the same upper quantile of the same response on common issue origins. The historical alternatives use past headrooms, paths translated to the current signed position, or native peaks floored at the observed current magnitude. The conditional alternatives use ridge quantile regression, nearest-neighbor quantiles and scaled nearest-neighbor quantiles.

The matched-history FX regression comparison lowers mean loss by 14.77\%, but increases breaches from 360 to 376. The original FX primary uses a different historical window and lowers loss by 12.66\%. The separately declared Treasury primary deteriorates by 50.79\%, with 54 rather than 28 breaches. Short-history FX regression also deteriorates at the longer horizon; a Treasury neighbor gain reverses on the sparse grid. These adverse outcomes are central findings.

The paper makes three contributions. First, it places established forecasting engines and historical constructions on a common completed-peak response with an explicit issue-known floor. Second, it controls completed-label pools and update schedules and retains the complete favorable and adverse model menu. Third, it documents how score, breach frequency, report coherence and fixed-report preferences can disagree across two financial measurement processes. The contribution is an application and model-validation benchmark using mature methods.

Section 2 locates the study in the literature. Sections 3--5 describe data, forecasts and evaluation. Sections 6--7 report FX and Treasury results. Section 8 collects exploratory robustness evidence, Section 9 discusses mechanisms and limitations, and Section 10 concludes. Detailed historical menus, geometry and supplementary diagnostics appear in the appendices.

\section*{2. Related literature}
Wisniewski, Lindsay and Lindsay (2020) and the net-position forecasting chapter of Wisniewski (2024) are the closest empirical lineage. They already study conditional, neighbor and normalized endpoint forecasts on the FX source family, using lagged positions and calendar information. Here the response is a single upper quantile of a future absolute sampled maximum, including the current magnitude. Marginal endpoint intervals and their averaged losses address a different functional; the present comparison fits the established engines directly to completed peak labels.

Financial path extrema have a substantial prior literature. MaxVaR evaluates worst intermediate mark-to-market loss (Boudoukh et al., 2004). Liao and Theodosopoulos (2005) study the timing of mark-to-market for collateralized contingent credit exposure. Van den Hoogen (2017) models a conditional intraday liquidity buffer through the maximum cumulative payment deficit; Petrunia, Sabetti and Voia (2019) study a cross-participant end-of-day debit maximum. Arjani, Li and Sabetti (2020) forecast remaining-day liquidity-demand ratios. These targets clarify the specific contribution of a sampled net-position envelope.

Regression quantiles (Koenker and Bassett, 1978), sequential neighbor quantiles (Biau and Patra, 2011), conditional historical filtering (Hull and White, 1998; Barone-Adesi et al., 1999), and quantile scoring (Gneiting, 2011) supply the mature methods. Quantile forests (Meinshausen, 2006), CAViaR (Engle and Manganelli, 2004), sequential conformal prediction (Xu and Xie, 2023), trajectory calibration (Zhou, Lindemann and Sesia, 2024) and expected-shortfall curves (Sözen, 2026) are further relevant alternatives. The executed estimator menu is deliberately bounded.

The resulting distinction is the measured peak response, known issue floor, completed-label timing, controlled history/update comparisons and qualified aggregate application. The benchmark measures how these mature procedures behave on the specified task; its supporting finite geometry explains construction differences.

\subsection*{Post-result / exploratory classical maximal-inequality benchmark}
Proposition 1 (classical Lévy bound, direct scalar application). Let the future real increments X\textsubscript{1},\ldots{},X\textsubscript{H} be independent and individually symmetric about zero, with S\textsubscript{h}=\(\sum\)\textsubscript{\(j=1\)}\textsuperscript{h}X\textsubscript{j}. They need not have the same distribution or finite moments. For a fixed starting position x, write \(B=|x|\) and q=inf\{u:Pr(|S\textsubscript{H}|\(\le\)u)\(\ge\)0.975\}. Lévy's maximal inequality implies the following strict-breach bound; Appendix J gives the proof. This is a classical result applied to this target, not a new theorem (Sussman, 2023, Proposition3.4).

\[
\Pr\!\left(\max_{0\le h\le H}|x+S_h|>B+q\right)\le\Pr\!\left(\max_{1\le h\le H}|S_h|>q\right)\le 2\Pr(|S_H|>q)\le0.05.
\]
The operational report L uses the same frozen completed-origin pool and refit times as F. Its endpoint sample is |N\textsubscript{i+H}\(-\)N\textsubscript{i}| and its one-based order rank is \(\lceil\)39(W+1)/40\(\rceil\). Add the resulting estimate to B\textsubscript{t}. This empirical plug-in is distinct from the known population quantile in Proposition1. Overlapping endpoint samples and dependent, changing series do not inherit the proposition's population coverage. Conditional coverage additionally requires the independence and symmetry premises and the correct endpoint quantile conditional on issue information. The bound supplies no pinball-loss ordering against F.

The fixed bandwidth is \(L=\max\{H,\lfloor4(n/100)^{2/9}\rfloor\}\); doubled bandwidth supplies a sensitivity check. Fixed finite estimation windows motivate the unconditional predictive-ability interpretation of Giacomini and White (2006), under mixing, adequate high-order moments and positive long-run variance. Shared training can extend dependence beyond the target horizon. These are working assumptions for this post-result analysis.

\[
DM=\frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\widehat\Omega/n}},\quad\widehat\Omega=\widehat\gamma_0+2\sum_{j=1}^L(1-j/(L+1))\widehat\gamma_j,\quad DM_{HLN}=DM\sqrt{\frac{n+1-2H+H(H-1)/n}{n}}.
\]

The hourly feature design transports awkwardly to the weekly Treasury task. Its 25 level coordinates span the current observation through 24 weeks of history. The two hour coordinates, two weekday coordinates and gap indicator are exactly constant on the weekly source. The original model has 33 predictors plus an intercept, or 34 coefficients, against \(W=52\) overlapping training labels in the shorter history. This is a high-dimensional fit relative to the available labels, rather than a \(p>n\) claim. All four Treasury penalty selections are menu endpoints. Its 52 validation origins contain at most 3 disjoint H24 label paths, a path count rather than an effective-sample-size estimate. Constant calendar coordinates, correlated levels, overlap and restricted tuning plausibly contribute to fragility; they remain hypotheses rather than causal findings.

\subsection*{Limitations}
The FX evaluation interval was previously inspected, and the subsequent robustness analyses are post-result / exploratory. These records do not restore a compatible unseen dealer sample. Treasury is a downloaded-vintage, economic-date aggregate replay rather than an original-release public-information backtest; cross-dealer netting, valuation and composition distinguish it from an individual dealer's book.

Shared histories, overlapping labels, finite validation and investigator selection limit statistical generalization. The known floor can create an outcome atom: a valid upper quantile need not have exactly the nominal strict-breach probability. Numerical acceptance supplies no conditional-coverage guarantee. The horizon-specific mature scenario sets differ, so a zero observed crossing count cannot establish general coherence.

Stipulated shortfall/excess weights are not observed financing prices. Quotes, fills, hedges, book decomposition, collateral and cash flows would be required to map this passive envelope into an operational inventory, margin or funding policy. This study evaluates forecasts, not such interventions; Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008) provide a distinct active inventory-sensitive quoting framework.

The strongest alternatives extend beyond the executed menu, including quantile forests, CAViaR, sequential conformal procedures and full volatility-filtered historical simulation. Same completed-label pools and update schedules improve procedural comparability while allowing differences in feature lookback, regularization, scaling and validation. Future compatible observations and decision-linked inputs would test broader portability.

A post-result / exploratory selected-fit readback examines the Treasury C2 menu boundary directly (Appendix I). At \(\lambda=10\), standardized response-normalized slope norms range from 0.001497 to 0.01937. Removing slopes while keeping each fitted intercept changes capacity by a mean absolute 136.8--832.3 source USD millions across the four cells. Relative to the lower empirical headroom-quantile report I, observed loss is 0.2432--2.192\% lower; this descriptive difference has no dedicated selection-adjusted test. The fits have small normalized slopes and high headroom correlation with I, but are not identical to I or F. A boundary penalty and high capacity correlation do not by themselves demonstrate zero feature value. Three of the four C2 cells still have higher loss than F.

The expanded aggregate panel strengthens the negative transport finding but does not isolate its mechanism. Features and tuning menus, finite sample size, target behavior and reporting-regime changes can all matter. Downloaded cross-era histories are not original-release vintages; metadata/provenance for each key are retained. A prospective public-release protocol freezes the four procedures and selected historical-validation penalties before future issue artifacts. The first planned new release is after the protocol freeze, rather than retroactively labeling the already published October14 observation as unseen. Because the release clock lags economic dates, the target includes prediction of unpublished measurements, with a nowcast/forecast mixture. Results await prior timestamped report issuance and target publication; no live prospective validation is claimed.

\section*{Appendix A. Finite geometry and its predictive limits}
On a common set and fixed rank, let \(d_{\rm abs}=\max_{i\in J}\bigl|B-|N_i|\bigr|\) and \(d_{\rm signed}=\max_{i\in J}|x-N_i|\). Elementary order-statistic and projection stability gives \(|F-K|\le d_{\rm abs}\), \(|S-K|\le d_{\rm signed}\), hence \(|F-S|\le d_{\rm abs}+d_{\rm signed}\). Appendix A proves these finite relationships and their predictive limits. Nearest signed-state membership minimizes its maximum signed distance at a given count; it need not minimize forecast loss. These statements do not automatically bound QR, scaled responses or the richer 33-coordinate distance.

\subsection*{A.1. Common-set projection bounds}
These construction arguments concern F/S/K on an identical historical set and rank. They are retained from the earlier comparison. A one-dimensional signed-distance minimax property does not extend automatically to the multivariate neighbor distance, and the bounds do not automatically constrain QR or scale-adjusted responses.

These are elementary finite-array arguments, rather than new asymptotic or coverage results. Fix a nonempty common selected set J, an available rank \(1\le k\le|J|\), query \(x=N_t\), floor \(B=|x|\) and completed historical windows. All identities in this appendix concern real arithmetic. Write \(B_i=|N_i|\), \(d_{i,h}=N_{i+h}-N_i\), with \(d_{i,0}=0\), and define

Let \(a_i=\min_h d_{i,h}\) and \(b_i=\max_h d_{i,h}\), so \(a_i\le0\le b_i\). These are the lower and upper increments denoted l and u in Section 4. The auxiliary nonnegative envelope coordinates below use \(u_i=b_i\) and \(v_i=-a_i\).

\[
A_i=B+P_i-B_i,\qquad T_i=\max_{0\le h\le H}|x+d_{i,h}|,\qquad C_B(z)=\max(B,z).
\]
Both \(A_i\) and \(T_i\) are at least B. The projection \(C_B\) is nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz. It commutes with a finite order statistic, as does a common translation. Hence \(F_J=Q_k(A)\), \(S_J=Q_k(T)\) and \(K_J=Q_k(C_B(P))\). Since \(C_B(A_i)=A_i\),

\[
|A_i-C_B(P_i)|\le |A_i-P_i|=|B-B_i|.
\]
The reverse triangle inequality bounds each path value's change under a starting-position translation by \(|x-N_i|\). Taking a maximum gives \(|T_i-P_i|\le|x-N_i|\). Applying the same floor projection preserves that bound because \(T_i\ge B\). Finally, paired order statistics are nonexpansive in the maximum coordinate difference: if \(|u_i-v_i|\le r\) for every i, then \(u_i\le v_i+r\) and conversely; monotonicity and common translation give \(|Q_k(u)-Q_k(v)|\le r\). These observations prove the two common-set K bounds stated above. The triangle inequality and \(\bigl||N_i|-|x|\bigr|\le|N_i-x|\) prove the stated F/S bound. Keeping the rank fixed while changing one side's historical rows does not by itself justify these common-set comparison bounds.

Among all size-m subsets, selecting the m smallest signed distances minimizes the largest selected distance: any alternative must include an element at least as far away as the mth ordered distance. This finite minimax fact, with the declared tie convention, concerns the signed radius. It does not minimize the absolute-anchor radius, the sum of the two radii, the actual report gap or a forecast loss. For every fixed realized y, pinball loss is \(\max(\tau,1-\tau)\)-Lipschitz in its report, so a report-gap bound also bounds the absolute loss difference. Such stability supplies no sign for the realized or expected loss difference.

\subsection*{A.2. Envelope plateaus and the role of signed anchors}
Put \(u_i=b_i\ge0\) and \(v_i=-a_i\ge0\). The headroom of an increment envelope at any anchor z is

\[
g_i(z)=\max(z+u_i,-z+v_i)-|z|=\begin{cases}\max(u_i,v_i-2z),&z\ge0,\\\max(u_i+2z,v_i),&z\le0.\end{cases}

\subsection*{A.4. Raw translation versus fixed-coefficient residual replay}
For interpretation, fix common coefficients c and \(\phi\) in \(N_{s+1}=c+\phi N_s+\epsilon_s\). Replay a historical window's ordered innovations from query x. \[
M_{i,h}(x)=N_{i+h}+\phi^h(x-N_i),\qquad \widetilde N^{tr}_{i,h}(x)=N_{i+h}+(x-N_i).

\[

\]

The identity needs no innovation law, while treating past innovations as representative of future conditional innovations is a separate assumption. \subsection*{AR estimation definition}
After the conditional results had been inspected, we specified one additional path-propagation comparison without an order, volatility or tuning menu. At each original refit \(\kappa\), put \(i_0=\kappa-H-W+1\).

\[
N_s=c_\kappa+\phi_\kappa N_{s-1}+\epsilon_s.
\]
Fit on the unique transitions \(i_0+1,\ldots,\kappa\). The W completed scenarios have \(W+H\) levels in their union and \(W+H-1\) unique transitions; overlapping paths do not duplicate transitions in OLS. Coefficients and the historical pool remain fixed until the next original refit, while the query uses the actual \(N_t\).

Using the same fitted coefficients for every residual in a block and replaying its original order from x=\(N_t\) gives the replay identity

\[
M_{i,h}(x)=N_{i+h}+\phi_\kappa^h(x-N_i).
\]
Set \(h=0\) explicitly to x and report the corrected empirical quantile of the W maximum absolute replay paths. The intercept cancels in this deterministic identity; it is still estimated in the mean recursion. At exact \(\phi_\kappa=1\) the arithmetic agrees with frozen S. Negative or above-one finite estimates are eligible, without clipping. Constant regressors, lost dispersion and nonfinite computations fail without a substitute model.

This is a mean-filtered ordered-block historical comparison, not the full conditional-volatility filtered simulation of Hull and White (1998) or Barone-Adesi et al. (1999). It does not standardize/rescale innovations, fit GARCH, independently draw future steps or introduce Monte Carlo randomness. Conditional representativeness of historical residual blocks remains unverified; numerical OLS acceptance supplies no coverage or mean-reversion law. Appendix A.4 gives the path relationship, and Appendix C records numerical checks.
